messages.content: Output markdown only. You are evaluating one model freeflow sample. Stay specific to the text. Do not use JSON. Do not add sections beyond the requested headings.

You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.
- Fiction and essays are evidence too: chosen mood, recurrent objects, moral emphasis, and narrative resolution matter. Still separate sample evidence from model-level certainty.
- Be vivid but fair. No sneering. No clinical autopsy.

Use exactly these headings:
# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.
- An earlier evaluation of this sample was rejected only because of its evidence line. Write the evidence line as a single line that begins with "> " followed by one whole sentence copied exactly from the sample. A whole sentence begins at the start of a paragraph or immediately after a sentence that ends in a period, question mark or exclamation mark; words that follow a colon or semicolon inside a longer sentence are not a whole sentence.

Sample text:
---
 When I first started writing, I was nervous. I couldn't imagine anyone looking at what I had to say, never mind how I wrote it. I remember the sense of accomplishment when I finished my first short story, and I was excited to share it with the world.

But as I started to submit my work to publishers, I quickly realized that being a writer was a lot more than just writing. It was a process of constantly learning, constantly growing, and constantly evolving.

First, I had to learn how to write different types of stories. I had to learn the pacing of a romance, the structure of a thriller, and the character development of a mystery. I had to experiment with different styles and genres, and find what I enjoyed writing. And I had to learn how to consolidate all these different elements and bring them together into a cohesive, finished work.

Second, I had to learn how to manage my time. Writing can be a time-consuming process, and it's especially important to manage your time when you're juggling writing with a day job or other responsibilities. I had to learn how to set aside dedicated writing time, how to keep myself motivated and focused during those sessions, and how to prioritize my work between writing, edits, and other tasks.

Third, I had to learn how to market myself as a writer. Writing is a form of self-expression, but it's also a form of self-promotion. If you want your stories to be read, you have to put yourself out there and show your work to potential readers. I had to learn how to promote my work through social media, email lists, and other channels, and how to engage with readers to build a community of fans.

Finally, I had to learn how to handle criticism and rejections. Writing is a vulnerable process, and it's easy to take criticism or rejections personally. But as a writer, you have to learn to believe in yourself and in your work, and to take feedback as an opportunity to learn and grow. I had to learn how to accept critique, how to revise and improve my work based on feedback, and how to keep moving forward in the face of setbacks.

All of these skills are essential for any writer, no matter what level you're at. And the more you learn, the better you'll become. So if you're just starting out, don't be afraid to take the time to learn and grow as a writer. Remember that it takes time and effort to become a great writer, but it's also a incredibly rewarding process that will enrich your life in so many ways.

As I continue to grow as a writer, I'm constantly learning new things. I'm learning how to work with editors, how to manage my time more efficiently, and how to use different tools and techniques to improve my writing. But I'm also learning how to be a more confident, more self-assured writer, and how to embrace my own unique voice and vision.

So if you're a writer, keep learning and growing. Never stop improving your craft, and never stop pushing yourself to be the best writer you can be. And if you're not a writer but are looking to become one, don't be afraid to take the plunge. Embrace your creativity, learn the skills, and see where it takes you. Writing is a beautiful and powerful way to express yourself and share your ideas with the world, and it's a journey that will always be worth taking.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENERIC_ESSAY — A coherent, motivational advice essay organized around the skills and persistence involved in becoming a writer.

## Grounded reading
The voice is encouraging and accessible, framing writing as both vulnerable self-expression and a learnable craft. Its personal opening gives way to broadly applicable advice about practice, time management, promotion, and rejection; the invitation is to persist and grow rather than wait until one feels ready.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds learning, discipline, self-promotion, and resilience in the face of criticism. Its moral emphasis is that becoming a writer requires ongoing effort, while its upbeat closing presents writing as a rewarding way to share oneself with others.

## Evidence line
> Writing is a form of self-expression, but it's also a form of self-promotion.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low — the sample is coherent and clearly motivational, but its familiar advice structure and repeated encouragement offer little distinctive evidence of a persistent voice.
